hasName.value_text: The Broomfield Depot Museum: Interpretive Materials
hasName.label: Name/Title

hasDescription.value_text: A 30-page history (15 front and back) of the Broomfield train depot, titled "The Broomfield Depot Museum: Interpretive Materials" compiled by Mary Ann McNair, February 2013. The history includes many aspects of the depot's history. The history begins with early contextual history of both Broomfield and of Colorado's railroads from the 1860s onward. It also lists the value of the dollar, popular books, movies, radio shows, inventions, and contemporary events from 1900 through 1940 in the United States to give a sense of the time period in which the depot operated. The latter half of the history describes the history of Broomfield's live-in depot and what life was like living there, along with timelines and family histories of all the agents who lived and/or worked there with their families from 1910 to 1949. The history also includes a table of contents and full list of sources.

hasDescription.value_text: The Proceedings and Papers of the Greenville County Historical Society, Volume IX (1990–1991) is a compilation of scholarly and commemorative works that highlight Greenville County’s rich historical tapestry. The volume includes archaeological insights on early Greenville through the Prospect Hill excavation, first-person accounts such as a 19th-century diary, and cultural analyses like the development of literary life and the legal profession. It also revisits the peaceful desegregation of Greenville County schools in 1970 and the evolution of the Greenville City Fire Department. Collectively, these articles preserve and present key elements of the county’s social, civic, and cultural development.

folders.name: 07. Southern Californian
folders.description:
This collection contains issues of the Southern Californian, a newspaper published in Lordsburg from of 1890 to 1892. Each issue runs the length of eight pages with a variety of news articles, current events, and advertisements. Topics include from religious editorials from members of the German Baptist Brethren Church, local land and agricultural ventures, and advertisements for machinery for orange growers. The citrus industry is clearly documented in the collection as a major component of the local economy. Prominent pioneer settlers such M.M. Eshelman and George McDonaugh appear throughout the Southern Californian. These members of the German Baptist Brethren Church gave the periodical its religious character. Another entity that played a role in the newspaper’s history, and the development of Lordsburg, was the Santa Fe Railroad, which appears in nearly every issue of this collection. The railroad even subsidized publication of the Southern Californian.

The Southern Californian offers modern readers contemporary insight into how Californians viewed the boom years of the nineteenth century, railroad, and the citrus industry. This newspaper, housed at Archives and Special Collections in Wilson Library of the University of La Verne, was recently digitized. Each page was scanned in grayscale at 300 dpi.

hasDescription.value_text:
Ebell bulletins from October 1903 to June 1927. The bulletins are small leaflets containing Announcements, Section Dates or Department Works, Programs, and Rules Concerning Guests or Notices. Starting in October 1908, issues included Officers and Directors. 

The 1920-1921 issues mention the formation of the Ebell Junior Auxiliary, the Welty Bill on immigration, the Disabled War Veteran Association, the Ebell's first Shakespearean Commemoration, and Save the Redwoods League.

Issues from October 1921 to June 1922 feature contributing pieces from members on the topics of American citizenship, national and international women's clubs, jury service, public schools, social work, scholarships, books and music, the Disarmament Conference, the Save the Redwoods League, the American School of Music in France, Roosevelt Day, the Ebell Rest Cottage, L.A. landmarks, and national parks. 

Issues from 1922-1923 cover the topics of the Chautauqua program, the International Conference of Settlement Workers, the California November ballot, the Red Cross, Disabled Veterans of the World War, the Rest Cottage, women's clubs, Save the Redwoods League, the Anderson Memorial Home, and a bond issue to build a central library in Los Angeles.

Fully digitized versions of the Ebell bulletins from 1921 to 1927 have been published on the Internet Archive.
hasDescription.label: Scope and Content

hasContext.value_text:
The Ebell was a monthly bulletin that first ran from 1903 to 1927 as a small pamphlet. The format changed to the Ebell Magazine, a larger format with articles and photos, which ran from October 1927 to December 1934. In January 1935, the Ebell returned to the condensed Bulletin format. 

The Ebell bulletins changed their name to the Ebell: Magazine of the Ebell of Los Angeles starting with the January 2007 issue. In October 2009, the publication shortened its name to Ebell Magazine. The bulletin format remained the same with the same content.

The club meeting location, Cumnock Hall, 1500 South Figueroa Street, appears on the cover of issues from 1903 to 1906.  The issues from 1907 to 1927 have the address of 1719 So. Figueroa Street. In the October 1921 issue, the Foreword announces an "amplified" bulletin which includes more contributors, with Mrs. John Stearns Thayer serving as the Bulletin Editor.
hasContext.label: Context

folders.name: 07. Southern Californian
folders.description:
This collection contains issues of the Southern Californian, a newspaper published in Lordsburg from of 1890 to 1892. Each issue runs the length of eight pages with a variety of news articles, current events, and advertisements. Topics include from religious editorials from members of the German Baptist Brethren Church, local land and agricultural ventures, and advertisements for machinery for orange growers. The citrus industry is clearly documented in the collection as a major component of the local economy. Prominent pioneer settlers such M.M. Eshelman and George McDonaugh appear throughout the Southern Californian. These members of the German Baptist Brethren Church gave the periodical its religious character. Another entity that played a role in the newspaper’s history, and the development of Lordsburg, was the Santa Fe Railroad, which appears in nearly every issue of this collection. The railroad even subsidized publication of the Southern Californian.

The Southern Californian offers modern readers contemporary insight into how Californians viewed the boom years of the nineteenth century, railroad, and the citrus industry. This newspaper, housed at Archives and Special Collections in Wilson Library of the University of La Verne, was recently digitized. Each page was scanned in grayscale at 300 dpi.

folders.name: North County and Rancho Santa Fe Living (1969–1972)
folders.description: This collection contains issues of North County and Rancho Santa Fe Living published between April 1969 and February 1972. The magazine functioned as a community and lifestyle publication, continuing Rancho Santa Fe Living under an expanded regional title and scope that incorporated broader North County San Diego coverage. Content includes residential properties, real estate activity, social events, and local organizations, along with editorial features and advertising reflecting the social and economic life of both Rancho Santa Fe and the surrounding region. The publication documents a period of transition in which the magazine broadened its geographic focus while maintaining consistent coverage of Rancho Santa Fe community life. Together, these issues provide insight into patterns of regional growth, residential marketing, and the social and cultural environment of North County San Diego during the early 1970s. The publication continues under the title San Diego’s North County Living beginning in March 1972. Click on the magazine cover image within each entry to open the complete, fully readable digital version of the issue.

hasDescription.value_text: Printed community magazine issue of North County and Rancho Santa Fe Living documenting residential life, social activity, and local institutions in Rancho Santa Fe and North County San Diego during October 1969. Primary editorial and named content includes Terry Esposito’s feature on the Roadrunner Club in Borrego Springs, emphasizing mobile home living, the executive golf course, clubhouse amenities, and air service access, as well as “Del Mar Yearling Sales … 1969,” coverage of the Whispering Palms Country Club opening benefit for the North Coast YMCA, “The Beat Goes On at Lomas Santa Fe,” and Lake San Marcos community reporting including “Par Tee Talk.” Association Bulletin and News is present and includes Rancho Santa Fe Association Board of Directors minutes and Rancho Santa Fe Art Jury proceedings addressing subdivision review, parcel approvals, architectural decisions, covenant matters, and governance actions. Riding and golf-related community coverage is present through Rancho Riding Club newsletter reporting, the Annual Golf Club Tournament Dinner Party, Los Rancheros planning for Fiesta Day, and Lomas Santa Fe junior and women’s golf events. Advertising and promotional content for real estate, retail, travel, home furnishings, and local services appears throughout the issue.

hasDescription.value_text: Printed community magazine issue of North County and Rancho Santa Fe Living documenting residential life, social activity, and local institutions in Rancho Santa Fe and North County San Diego during February 1970. Primary editorial and feature content includes the illustrated special feature “Palm Springs Aerial Tramway: The Impossible Dream,” detailing the development, financing, and engineering challenges of the Mt. San Jacinto tramway project, including early advocacy by Francis Crocker and later state-supported construction efforts. Additional editorial content includes “The In Set” by Terry Esposito covering regional social events, including gatherings at the Half Moon Inn and participation by Rancho Santa Fe residents, along with profiles and features such as Paula Kent’s public relations career and civic involvement. The issue also contains extensive regional coverage of La Jolla as “The Seaside Jewel,” including civic institutions, cultural organizations, educational facilities, and commercial activity. Association Bulletin and News includes Rancho Santa Fe Association Board of Directors minutes and Rancho Santa Fe Art Jury proceedings addressing governance, architectural review, subdivision oversight, and community planning matters. Additional content includes Rancho Santa Fe School coverage, animal and recreational features, and extensive advertising for real estate, retail, and financial services.

folders.description: This collection contains issues of San Diego’s North County Living published between March 1972 and February 1977. The magazine functioned as a community and lifestyle publication serving Rancho Santa Fe and the broader North County San Diego region, continuing the publication previously issued as North County and Rancho Santa Fe Living. Content includes residential properties, real estate activity, social events, local organizations, dining and entertainment coverage, editorial features, and commercial advertising reflecting the social, cultural, and economic life of North County communities during the 1970s. While the publication expanded its regional identity and coverage, Rancho Santa Fe remained a recurring focus throughout the run. Together, these issues document patterns of suburban development, community identity, residential marketing, and social life across North County San Diego during a period of continued regional growth and change. Click on the magazine cover image within each entry to open the complete, fully readable digital version of the issue.

hasDescription.value_text: Printed community and lifestyle magazine issue of San Diego’s North County Living documenting North County San Diego social organizations, resort culture, equestrian activities, real estate development, banking expansion, arts programming, charitable fundraising, and regional leisure culture during February 1973. Featured content includes “Living Around Town” by Terry Esposito, “A Ski Vacation in the French Alps,” “Inklings” by Pat Britt, “Apeeling Seens O’Side” by Kitty Peeling, “Restaurant Row,” “Shoppers Bazaar,” and “Association News.” Major coverage documents La Costa social and sports events surrounding the Andy Williams-San Diego Open, San Luis Rey Academy Mardi Gras fundraising activities, Santa Fe Hunt Club social events, Rancho Santa Fe Golf Club activities, California Professional Horsemen’s Association awards, Olympic athlete Bob Beamon’s work with the Special Olympics for the Retarded, West Coast National Bank expansion, Home Federal Savings and Loan growth, and contemporary cultural programming at the La Jolla Museum of Contemporary Art and Reuben H. Fleet Space Theater. Additional content reflects luxury residential marketing, mobile home communities, fashion retail, banking services, desert resort promotion, equestrian culture, golf, tennis, skiing tourism, fine dining, and commercial advertising throughout Rancho Santa Fe, La Jolla, Del Mar, Carlsbad, Oceanside, Escondido, Borrego Springs, and the broader North County region.
